passages.happening:
Sarai has had no children. She has an Egyptian servant named Hagar (verse 1).

Sarai says to Abram, “Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.” “And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai” (verse 2). After ten years in Canaan, Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife (verse 3).

Hagar becomes pregnant, and she begins to look down on Sarai (verse 4). Sarai blames Abram: “May the wrong done to me be upon you!” (verse 5).

Abram answers, “your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her” (verse 6). “Then Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that she fled from her” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Hagar is an enslaved woman. She belongs to Sarai. She is given to Abram to bear a child for someone else. She has no say in any of it. Her body is used for another woman's plan.

In that world this was a known custom. The Laws of Hammurabi, a Babylonian law code from about 1754 BC, have rules for a case like it: a wife who could not bear children gives her husband a slave woman to bear them. The same laws say that if the slave mother then claims to be equal with her mistress, she may be put back among the slaves, but if she has borne children she may not be sold. The parallel is real but not exact. (Tablets from Nuzi, in northern Iraq, have also been compared with this story, but scholars now use those comparisons with caution.)

A child born this way counted as the wife's child. Sarai's words ‘build a family’ play on the Hebrew words for ‘son’ and ‘build’. She hopes to get a son through Hagar.

Notice the names. Sarai calls Hagar ‘my maidservant’ and ‘my servant’. Abram calls her ‘your servant’. Neither of them ever says her name.

And notice Abram. When Sarai speaks, he listens, the same words used of Adam in 3:17. When trouble comes, he steps aside: do whatever you want with her. He does nothing to protect the pregnant woman carrying his child.
passages.later:
Paul looks back on Abraham's two sons in Galatians: “Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman” (Galatians 4:22). The note on verses 13-16 explains how he uses the story.

The Bible's later law says something striking about runaway slaves: “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15).

God says at the burning bush, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt” (Exodus 3:7). Here it is an Egyptian woman who is mistreated in Abram's house. Later Abram's own family will be mistreated in Egypt. The God who sees the one sees the other.
passages.hard:
Does the Bible approve of what was done to Hagar? No. Genesis tells it as it happened, but telling is not the same as approving.

The story shows the harm the plan causes. Hagar despises Sarai. Sarai blames Abram. Abram hands Hagar over. Sarai treats her so harshly that a pregnant woman runs into the desert rather than stay. Nothing in the chapter calls this good. The plan was Sarai's idea, carried out by Abram, and the person who paid for it was Hagar.

Sarai is not a villain with no story. She has waited years for a child, in a world that made a childless wife feel like a failure. Her pain is real. But her pain does not excuse her harshness. Hagar was in her power, and she used that power to hurt her.

The Bible does not hide that its great families held slaves and used them. It shows us the harm, so that we can see it. And the rest of this chapter shows whose side God is on.
passages.asks: Sarai and Abram tried to get God's promise by their own plan, and someone with no power paid the price. Ask whether you have ever pushed a plan through that cost someone else more than it cost you. Then ask who in your life has no say, and whether you have noticed them.

passages.happening:
“Now the angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert” (verse 7), on the road to Shur.

He speaks to her by name: “Hagar, servant of Sarai,” he said, “where have you come from, and where are you going?” She answers, “I am running away from my mistress Sarai” (verse 8).

The angel says, “Return to your mistress and submit to her authority” (verse 9). Then he adds a promise: “I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count” (verse 10).

She is carrying a son, and she is to name him Ishmael, “for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction” (verse 11). Ishmael means ‘God hears’. He will be “a wild donkey of a man”, free and hard to tame (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Shur was on the road toward Egypt. Hagar is going home.

The angel of the LORD is God's messenger, and in this story he speaks with God's own voice. He is the first person in the story to call Hagar by her name. And he asks her two questions, as if her own account of her life matters: where have you come from, and where are you going?

God gives promises to Hagar that sound like the promises to Abram. Her offspring will be too many to count. Her son has a name from God.

The ‘wild donkey’ is the onager, a desert animal that could not be tamed. To us the phrase sounds like an insult. To Hagar, a slave, it meant something else: her son would never be anyone's slave. He would live free in the open country. The next words, that he will live at odds with his brothers, describe a hard and independent life.

This verse is about one man. It is not a judgment on any people today. It has sometimes been used to speak badly of Arabs. That is a misuse of Scripture, and these notes reject it.
passages.later:
The same pattern comes back in Hagar's story. Years later, when she and Ishmael are sent away for good, “God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven” (Genesis 21:17). God opens her eyes to a well of water (Genesis 21:19), and “God was with the boy” (Genesis 21:20).

The psalms pray to the same God who sees and hears: “O LORD, You have searched me and known me” (Psalm 139:1). The God who hears is the God who sees.
passages.hard:
“Return to your mistress and submit to her authority” (verse 9). This is one of the hardest lines in Genesis, and it should not be softened. Hagar has been used and treated harshly, and God's messenger sends her back to the woman who hurt her. Israel's own later law says, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15). The tension is real.

Readers answer it in different ways. Many point out that a pregnant woman alone in the desert was likely to die, so going back kept her and her son alive. The command comes joined to promises that belong to her alone, and to a son who will never be a slave. Others note that the return is not forever: in chapter 21 she leaves for good, and God is with her there too. The theologian Delores S. Williams, in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993), read Hagar's story as God helping the oppressed to survive and to make a life, even where he does not yet set them free. The text does not answer every question, and these notes will not pretend it does.

This verse is not a command for anyone today to go back to a person who is hurting them. It was a word to one woman, in one desert, about one unborn child. No one should use it to send a wife, a child, a worker or anyone else back to harm.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The angel asked Hagar, ‘Where have you come from, and where are you going?’ Ask yourself the same two questions. Then remember that the God who asked them was not angry with her. He came looking for her.

passages.happening:
Hagar gives a name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the God who sees me.” For she said, “Here I have seen the One who sees me!” (verse 13).

The well is named Beer-lahai-roi, between Kadesh and Bered (verse 14).

“And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne” (verse 15). Abram is eighty-six years old (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Hagar names God. In Hebrew the name is El Roi, ‘the God who sees me’ or ‘the God of seeing’. The name is found nowhere else in the Bible. She is one of very few people in the Bible who give God a name, and many readers say she is the only one. Others name places and altars after what God did. Hagar names God himself, and she names him for what he did for her: he saw her.

The second half of the verse is one of the hardest lines in Genesis to translate. Bibles render it in different ways. It may mean she has seen God and lived, or that she has seen the One who sees her. Either way, the point is clear. The slave nobody called by name has been seen by God.

Beer-lahai-roi is usually explained as ‘the well of the Living One who sees me’. Isaac later lives near it (Genesis 24:62; 25:11). The family that used Hagar ends up drinking from the well she named.

Then Hagar comes back, and the son is born. Abram names him Ishmael, the name the angel gave. It seems Hagar told Abram what she heard in the desert, and he listened.
passages.later:
Ishmael is not forgotten. God promises to bless him and make him a great nation (Genesis 17:20). When Abraham dies, “His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him” (Genesis 25:9).

Paul uses this story in Galatians 4:21-31. He says plainly that he is using it as a picture: “These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants” (Galatians 4:24). In his picture, Hagar stands for slavery and Mount Sinai, and Sarah for freedom and “the Jerusalem above” (Galatians 4:26). He is writing to non-Jewish Christians who were being told they must keep the law of Moses to belong to God. His point is that belonging to God comes by God's promise, not by human effort.
passages.hard:
Two things should be said clearly.

First, Paul's use of Hagar in Galatians 4 is his argument about his own day, made with a picture. It is not a verdict on Hagar the woman, who in Genesis is seen, named and blessed by God. And it is not a verdict on Jewish people. The same Paul writes, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). He says of Israel, “Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants” (Romans 9:4). His quarrel was with those who said Gentile Christians had to become Jewish to belong to God.

Second, Ishmael and Islam. Muslims honor Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael. In Islamic tradition Ishmael (in Arabic, Ismail) is a prophet, and he is remembered as an ancestor of the Arabs and of the prophet Muhammad. The Qur'an does not name Hagar (in Arabic, Hajar), but Muslim tradition tells how she ran between two hills near Mecca, Safa and Marwa, looking for water for her son, until God gave them water from the spring called Zamzam. Pilgrims to Mecca still walk between those two hills to remember her. Christians and Muslims tell Hagar's story differently, and they differ on deep things. But Christians can say with respect what Genesis itself says: God saw Hagar, heard her son, and blessed him. These notes say nothing against Arabs or Muslims.
passages.asks: Hagar, the one nobody named, gave God a name: the God who sees me. Ask whether you feel unseen, at home, at work or at church. Then ask who around you is unseen, and whether you could be the one who calls them by name.
